2.text: firmly into the ice, and clutched it with both hands, trying to stand his

3.text: ground against the sea. The sea was rough, the waves rolled over his head,

4.text: and he was thoroughly drenched. After several hours of such suffering,

5.text: Kaˊtek rebelled against his fate, and he was about to end the ordeal by

6.text: stabbing himself with his belt-knife, when a large walrus-head suddenly

7.text: popped out of the water quite close to him, and sang, “O Kaˊtek, do not

8.text: kill yourself! You shall again see the mountains of Uñiˊsak and the little

9.text: Kuwaˊkak, your elder son.” Then, quite unexpectedly, Kaˊtek saw a large

10.text: iceberg, which drew the block on which he stood towards itself. Most

11.text: icebergs are quite steep and inaccessible, but on this one he found a gentle

12.text: slope where he could easily land. He took his harpoon along, and, hauling

13.text: in the line, found the harpoon-point still fast to the seal-carcass. After that

14.text: he climbed the iceberg, and, finding a suitable place, constructed a temporary

15.text: shelter of the blocks of rough ice lying about. Then he skinned the seal,

16.text: and, creeping under the shelter, spread the skin for a floor-covering, and,

17.text: crouching down, took off his clothes piece by piece, carefully wringing out

18.text: the water, and scraping it off with his knife. He ate of the seal-blubber, and

19.text: swallowed a few pieces of ice, which tasted like fresh water. Then the wind

20.text: changed and the iceberg drifted to land. At last, after more than twenty-four

21.text: hours spent on the water, he came to land near the village of Čeˊčin. When

22.text: he reached his own village, he found his family were already bringing sacrifice

23.text: of seal-oil to his manes. He bade them direct the sacrifice to the walrus-

24.text: head, and from that time on he was a shaman. He had some renown among

25.text: his neighbors, and his art was in requisition in the village of Uñiˊsak.

26.text: There is a limit, however, as to the age at which a person may become

27.text: a shaman, even with due call and occasion. In the case of Aiñanwaˊt, he

28.text: was more than forty, and felt his soul unfit for a change.

29.text: In a Koryak tale, when Quikɪnn˙aˊqu unexpectedly makes for himself a

30.text: drum out of a small louse, and becomes a shaman, his neighbors say scepti-

31.text: cally, “Has the old Quikɪnn˙aˊqu really become a shaman? From his youth

32.text: up he had no spirits within his call.”¹

33.text: Though this instance is taken from the Koryak, and that of Kaˊtek from

34.text: the Aiwan Eskimo, both answer the purpose equally well, since the shamanism

35.text: of the Chukchee and of these two tribes has similar features.

36.text: It is also considered perfectly natural that a young boy visited by some

37.text: great misfortune should try to call to the “spirits.” If they deign to come

38.text: to his assistance, their fellowship with the boy is likely to become very in-

39.text: timate, and he has the chance of being a really great shaman.

40.text: Thus a shaman, by name Scratching-Woman, told me that his father

41.text: was a small, sickly fellow, who had but a few reindeer, which he finally lost

42.text: in a thick fog, not far from the Russian village of Markova. He and his
